**Brief: TCC work plan (4 pages, Portuguese), "Grafos Multicamadas para Preservação de Consistência em Diálogos Multiagente"**

**(1) Identification**
- Title: *Grafos Multicamadas para Preservação de Consistência em Diálogos Multiagente* (p. 1).
- Authors (a pair): Rafael da Silva Estrela (matrícula 2312130005) and Manoel Matheus Correia dos Anjos (matrícula 2122130045) (p. 1).
- Advisor: Prof. Roger Rocha Ferreira (p. 1).
- Institution: Instituto de Educação Superior de Brasília (IESB), Direção Acadêmica, Coordenação de TCC. The form is a "Plano de Trabalho Individual" for TCC (p. 1).
- The course name is not stated. The schedule is for semester 2026/02 and mentions "TCC II" as a later stage (p. 2).
- The signature date and the start and end dates are blank (pp. 1, 3).

**(2) Problem, objectives, justification**
- Summary: The plan is to implement a narrative system. Multiple LLM-based agents talk to each other and to the user to produce a continuous, coherent plot. Each agent knows who it is, including its experiences, relationships, and personality (p. 1).
- Justification: Multi-agent AI is used in interactive narratives, investigation games, and negotiation simulations. In these, coherence requires each participant to keep its past experiences, knowledge limits, and individuality over time. Linear text approaches fail to retain long histories at low computational cost. Multilayer graph architectures such as MAGMA are an alternative. The study's importance is extending MAGMA from a single agent to multiple agents with individual perspectives and restricted information (p. 1).
- Problem: With independent agents, the shared knowledge base is constantly updated. This requires validation so that confidential data is not shared. Answers must also be correct, produced in acceptable time, and use reasonable resources (p. 1).
- General objective: Adapt the MAGMA architecture to preserve the coherence of LLM-generated multi-agent narratives. This should make long plots possible even when they contain lies, secrets, and different points of view (p. 1).
- Specific objectives (pp. 1–2):
  1. Model the memory graph so that real events are separated from mere character statements.
  2. Implement visibility rules on database nodes so each agent accesses only the facts it witnessed.
  3. Develop contradiction detection in the history, to update the status of past statements when new facts appear.
  4. Evaluate narrative coherence and computational efficiency, comparing the solution with traditional memory approaches.

**(3) Methodology**
- Process: Weekly meetings on Fridays at 19h. They cover progress and technical output. They also document how changes to the system model affected the benchmark results (p. 2).
- Build: A prototype that extends the MAGMA reference source code (MIT license). It is compared against MAGMA and a third-party RAG implementation (p. 2).
- Activities (p. 3):
  - Proof of concept: a simplified implementation integrating a graph database with the LLM agents.
  - Tests: dialogues in controlled scenarios, testing context retention and secret privacy.
  - Comparative analysis: token consumption, response time, logical consistency, and memory integrity.
- Metrics named: token consumption, response time, logical consistency, memory integrity (p. 3). Coherence and efficiency are the evaluation axes (p. 2).
- Datasets: none are specified. The plan says "benchmarks" (p. 2) and "controlled scenarios" (p. 3) but names no concrete dataset. DEBATE is cited only as a "reference to test" secrets and viewpoints (p. 2).
- The plan gives no details on the graph database, the LLM models, or the contradiction-detection algorithm.

**(4) Relation to MAGMA and related work (p. 2, also p. 1)**
- MAGMA (Jiang et al., 2026), *A Multi-Graph based Agentic Memory Architecture for AI Agents*. It organizes long-term memory into four graph layers: temporal, entities, causal, and semantic. It is "the basic structure adapted in this project" (p. 2).
- MAGMA was designed for a single agent. The project extends it to multiple agents with asymmetric information and secrecy (p. 1).
- The "Requisitos da adaptação" step maps MAGMA's limitations for multiple agents. It also specifies the requirements for information asymmetry and secrecy (p. 3).
- The "Estudo inicial" step is a literature review focused on MAGMA and relational memory structures (p. 3).
- MAGMA is also a comparison baseline, and the plan expects to preserve the long-term retention and logical consistency of MAGMA's original layers (p. 2).
- Other works and the role each plays in the plan (p. 2):
  - AdaMARP (Xu et al., 2026): separates real physical actions from what characters only say. It is the basis for distinguishing facts from statements in the graph.
  - DEBATE (Chuang et al., 2025): a benchmark of whether agents keep their own opinions over long conversations. It is a reference for testing secrets and viewpoints.
  - ToMAgent (Zhou et al., 2024): Theory of Mind, modeling what each agent knows or ignores about others. It grounds the secrecy and privacy rules.
  - "Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved: Graph Memory for LLM Agents" (Ji et al., 2026): shows that retrieval from structured graphs uses fewer resources than linear text in long dialogues. It is the basis for measuring token savings and response time.

**(5) Schedule and deliverables (pp. 2–3), semester 2026/02, 20 weeks**
- Estudo inicial: weeks 4, 5, 8.
- Requisitos da adaptação: weeks 8–9.
- Modelagem: week 10.
- Prova de conceito: weeks 10–11.
- Testes: weeks 12–13.
- Análise comparativa: week 13.
- Relatório parcial: week 14.
- Gravação (explanatory video): weeks 15 and 16.
- Apresentação oral (defense before the examining board): week 16.
- Ajustes para TCC II: weeks 16–17.
- Deadlines (p. 3):
  - Introduction: 09/10/2026.
  - Method: 23/10/2026.
  - End of data collection: 30/10/2026.
  - End of data analysis: 04/11/2026.
  - Results: 06/11/2026.
  - Discussion: 10/11/2026.
  - Final TCC version: 13/11/2026.
  - Defense preview: 27/11/2026.
- In-person meetings are on Fridays from 19:00 to 21:00, on 02/10, 09/10, 16/10, 23/10, 30/10, 06/11, 13/11, 20/11, and 29/11 (p. 3). Note that 29/11 is listed in the document but is not a Friday.
- The partial report is to contain the introduction, theoretical support, methodology, test results, and next steps (p. 3).

**(6) References** (cited in the "Suporte teórico" section, p. 2; there is no separate reference list)
- Jiang et al., 2026 (MAGMA).
- Xu et al., 2026 (AdaMARP).
- Chuang et al., 2025 (DEBATE).
- Zhou et al., 2024 (ToMAgent).
- Ji et al., 2026 (Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved).

**(7) Research questions and hypotheses**
- No formal research questions or hypotheses are stated. The "Resultados esperados" section (p. 2) gives implicit hypotheses:
  - H1: Separating real events from statements, combined with node-level visibility rules, prevents secret leakage and sustains individual viewpoints throughout the plot.
  - H2: The multi-agent adaptation preserves MAGMA's long-term retention and the logical consistency of its original layers.
  - H3: The solution will use fewer tokens and have lower response time than traditional memory approaches.

**What the student commits to:** extending MAGMA's four-layer graph memory into a multi-agent narrative system with three additions:
- a facts-versus-statements distinction;
- per-agent node visibility rules;
- contradiction detection.

They then evaluate it against MAGMA and a third-party RAG baseline on token use, latency, logical consistency, memory integrity, and secret privacy (pp. 1–3).

- **Code:** https://github.com/FredJiang0324/MAGMA (pp. 1–3).
- **Funding:** NSF grants 2343863, 2413520, 2417747 and 2440611 (p. 9).

## (2) Problem, motivation, hypotheses
- **LLM limits:**
  - LLMs have a finite attention window.
  - Their internal state does not persist across interactions.
  - Attention degrades with distance: "lost-in-the-middle" and context decay.
  - They have no native structured memory (p. 1).
- **Memory-Augmented Generation (MAG):**
  - MAG adds an external, persistent, queryable memory that is continuously updated (p. 1).
  - Unlike static RAG, it has a time-variant memory M_t. The paper writes this as o_t = LLM(q_t, Retrieve(q_t, M_t)) (Eq. 1) and M_{t+1} = Update(M_t, q_t, o_t) (Eq. 2) (p. 2).
  - Figure 1 shows this loop: the agent LLM, the user/environment, and a dynamic memory with retrieval and update (p. 2).
- **Problem with current MAG systems:**
  - Most use monolithic or minimally structured stores. They retrieve by semantic similarity, recency or heuristics (p. 1).
  - This entangles temporal, causal and entity information. It hurts interpretability and the alignment between query intent and retrieved evidence, so reasoning accuracy suffers (p. 1, abstract).
  - Examples given: A-Mem uses Zettelkasten-like notes but retrieves by embedding similarity, so it misses temporal and causal relations. Nemori does episodic segmentation, but its memory is "narrative and undifferentiated" (pp. 1–2).
  - Prior work organizes memory by "associative proximity" rather than "mechanistic dependency". Such systems can retrieve *what* happened but struggle with *why* (p. 3).
- **Hypothesis (implicit):** Explicitly modelling orthogonal relational views, plus intent-aware traversal, gives more accurate, efficient and interpretable long-horizon reasoning. The paper states no formal numbered research questions.

## (3) Claimed contributions (p. 2)
1. **MAGMA:** a multi-graph agentic memory architecture modelling semantic, temporal, causal and entity relations.
2. **Adaptive Traversal Policy:** it routes retrieval by query intent and prunes irrelevant graph regions. The authors claim lower latency and fewer tokens.
3. **Dual-stream memory evolution:** latency-sensitive event ingestion (fast path) is separated from asynchronous structural consolidation (slow path).
4. **Empirical results:** consistently better than state-of-the-art agentic memory on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, with lower retrieval latency and token use. Code is open-sourced.

## (4) Methodology (Section 3, pp. 3–6; Appendix B–C)

### 3.1 Three layers (Fig. 2, p. 3)
- **Query Process:** Intent-Aware Router → Adaptive Topological Retrieval → Context Synthesizer.
- **Data Structure Layer:** a vector database plus four relation graphs (semantic, temporal, causal, entity).
- **Write/Update Process:** Synaptic Ingestion (fast path) and Asynchronous Consolidation (slow path).

### 3.2 Data structure (p. 4)
- **Graph:** a time-variant directed multigraph G_t = (N_t, E_t). Nodes are events and edges are heterogeneous relations.
- **Event node (Eq. 3):** n_i = ⟨c_i, τ_i, v_i, A_i⟩.
  - c_i is the content.
  - τ_i is a discrete timestamp.
  - v_i ∈ R^d is a dense embedding indexed in a vector DB (FAISS, Johnson et al. 2019).
  - A_i is metadata: entity references, temporal cues and so on. It enables hybrid retrieval.
  - Nodes are described as multi-granular, from atomic events to episodic groupings.
- **Edge subspaces:**
  - **Temporal:** ordered pairs with τ_i < τ_j. This is an immutable chain that serves as the "ground truth" for chronology.
  - **Causal:** directed edges for logical entailment. An edge exists if S(n_j|n_i,q) > δ. The consolidation module infers these edges, and they serve "Why" queries.
  - **Semantic:** undirected edges where cos(v_i, v_j) > θ_sim.
  - **Entity:** links events to abstract entity nodes. This addresses "object permanence" across disjoint timeline segments.

### 3.3 Query process: adaptive hierarchical retrieval (pp. 4–6; Fig. 3 on p. 5; Algorithm 1 on p. 5)
- **Stage 1 — query analysis.** A Router R extracts three things:
  - An intent class T_q ∈ {WHY, WHEN, ENTITY}, from a "lightweight classifier". It acts as the "steering wheel".
  - A temporal parse [τ_s, τ_e], where a temporal tagger resolves relative expressions ("last Friday") into absolute time windows.
  - A dense query embedding q⃗ and sparse keywords q_key.
- **Stage 2 — anchor identification.** Dense, lexical and temporal signals are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al. 2009). Eq. 4: S_anchor = TopK Σ_{m∈{vec,key,time}} 1/(k + r_m(n)).
- **Stage 3 — Adaptive Traversal Policy.** This is a heuristic beam search from the anchors.
  - Transition score (Eq. 5): S(n_j|n_i,q) = exp(λ1·φ(type(e_ij),T_q) + λ2·sim(n⃗_j,q⃗)).
  - Structural alignment (Eq. 6): φ(r,T_q) = w_{T_q}ᵀ·1_r. Here w_{T_q} is an intent-specific weight vector and 1_r is the one-hot edge type.
  - Example: CAUSAL edges get high weight for WHY queries.
  - Algorithm 1: frontier expansion up to MaxDepth. The cumulative score is score_v = score_u·γ + s_uv, with decay γ. The beam keeps the top-k per step. Traversal stops when a visited-node budget is reached.
- **Stage 4 — narrative synthesis via graph linearization:**
  1. *Topological ordering.* WHEN queries are sorted by timestamp. WHY queries are topologically sorted on causal edges, so causes precede effects.
  2. *Context scaffolding with provenance (Eq. 7).* Each node becomes `<t:τ_i> content <ref:id>`, and these are concatenated. This is meant to reduce hallucination and make the LLM "an interpreter of evidence rather than a creative writer".
  3. *Salience-based token budgeting.* Scores from Eq. 5 set a dynamic budget. Low-salience nodes are collapsed into "brevity codes" (e.g., "...3 intermediate events...").

### 3.4 Memory evolution: dual stream (pp. 6–7; Algorithms 2–3 on p. 6)
- **Rationale:** it is motivated by Complementary Learning Systems theory (Kumaran et al. 2016).
- **Fast path, "synaptic ingestion" (Alg. 2):**
  - Segment the event.
  - Add a temporal edge from the previous node.
  - Compute the embedding and add it to the vector DB.
  - Enqueue the node ID.
  - No blocking LLM reasoning happens here.
- **Slow path, "structural consolidation" (Alg. 3, Eq. 8):**
  - A background worker dequeues node IDs.
  - It takes the 2-hop neighborhood.
  - It prompts an LLM Φ to infer E_new = Φ_reason(N(n_t), H_history).
  - It adds the resulting Causal and Entity edges. The paper describes this as trading compute time for relational depth.

### 3.5 Implementation (p. 6)
- Three layers: storage, retrieval and application.
- The storage layer abstracts typed graph, dense-vector and sparse-keyword backends. Backends are swappable, e.g. in-memory versus production graph/vector DBs.
- Utility modules handle episodic segmentation and temporal normalization.

### Hyperparameters (Table 6, p. 13)
These were "empirically optimized on the LoCoMo benchmark".

| Group | Setting |
|---|---|
| Embedding | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d, default); text-embedding-3-small (1536-d, optional) |
| LLM | gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.0 |
| Retrieval | RRF k = 60; vector top-K = 20; keyword fusion weight 2.0–5.0; similarity threshold 0.10–0.30 |
| Traversal | max depth 5 hops; max nodes 200; drop threshold 0.15 |
| Adaptive weights | λ1 = 1.0 (base); λ2 = 0.3–0.7 |
| Intent weights | w_entity 2.5–6.0; w_temporal 0.5–4.0; w_causal 3.0–5.0; w_phrase 2.5–5.0 |

- The beam width and γ are not given in Table 6 (the extracted text shows none).

### Prompts (Appendix C, pp. 13–14)
- **Event extraction:** a strict-JSON prompt that returns entities, topic, relationships, semantic_facts, dates_mentioned and summary.
- **Adaptive QA prompt:**
  - It answers only from context. If the answer is absent it must say "Information not found". Answers are concise (1–10 words).
  - It injects a dynamic instruction chosen by the router: Multi-hop, Temporal (output dates as "D Month YYYY"), Open-domain/inference, or Single-hop.
  - The authors state this uses no oracle labels.
- **LLM-judge prompt:**
  - It scores 0.0–1.0 on the scale 1.0 / 0.8 / 0.6 / 0.4 / 0.2 / 0.0.
  - It accepts relative times that resolve to the same period.
  - For adversarial "Unanswerable" gold answers, any hallucinated fact scores 0.

### Alternatives mentioned
- Optional OpenAI embeddings.
- Swappable storage backends.
- The graph-schema flexibility discussed in the case study (p. 15).
- No explicit design-alternative comparisons (e.g., a different traversal algorithm) are reported beyond the ablations.

## (5) Datasets (pp. 6–7, 15)
- **LoCoMo** (Maharana et al. 2024): ultra-long multi-session conversations, "average length of 9K tokens". It targets long-range temporal and causal retrieval.
  - The full benchmark was used, with five categories (Table 7, p. 15): Single-Hop 841, Adversarial 446, Temporal 321, Multi-Hop 282, Open-Domain 96. The total is 1,986 questions.
  - No train/test split is described. Nothing is trained, but hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo (p. 13).
- **LongMemEval** (Wu et al. 2024): a stress-test benchmark with average context over 100K tokens. Six question types appear in Table 2 (p. 8). The paper gives no question counts or split information.
- **Preprocessing:** event segmentation, LLM JSON extraction, and temporal normalization. For example, "yesterday" is resolved to a date at ingestion (pp. 15–16).

## (6) Metrics and baselines
- **Primary metric:** LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al. 2023). The judge is gpt-4o-mini at temperature 0, with the rubric above (pp. 7, 14, 15).
- **Secondary metrics:** token-level F1 and BLEU-1 (Papineni et al. 2002). No formulas are given (p. 7).
- **Systems metrics:** memory build time (hours), tokens per query (k), and query latency (s) (p. 8).
- **Baselines (p. 7):**
  - Full Context (the whole history in the prompt, up to gpt-4o-mini's 128k limit).
  - A-MEM (Zettelkasten-like, self-evolving).
  - Nemori ("predict-calibrate" episodic segmentation; the paper calls it graph-based).
  - MemoryOS (hierarchical storage OS).
- **Fairness protocol (p. 15):** the same gpt-4o-mini backbone for all, official default hyperparameters for baselines, and identical judge settings.
- **Metric validation (Appendix F, pp. 16–18):**
  - Table 10 gives seven hand-built cases where F1/BLEU-1 give false rewards or false penalties.
  - "compatible" vs "not compatible" gets F1 0.857. "John" vs "Sarah" gets 0.750. "14:00" vs "2 PM" gets 0.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Nemori | 0.569 | 0.649 | 0.485 | 0.764 | 0.325 | 0.590 |
| **MAGMA** | 0.528 | 0.650 | 0.517 | 0.776 | 0.742 | **0.700** |

| **Average** | 55.0% | 56.2% | **61.2%** |

|---|---|---|---|

|---|---|
| Nemori | 0.502 / 0.403 |

1. **LLM-dependent graph quality.** Consolidation relies on LLM inference, so extraction errors and hallucinations can create spurious or missing edges and propagate downstream. The authors cite structured prompts and "conservative inference thresholds" as mitigation.

3. **Narrow evaluation.** Only conversational and agentic benchmarks are covered. Extending to multimodal agents or heterogeneous observation streams "may require additional adaptation and calibration" (future work).

- Hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo, which is also the main test set.
- A single backbone (gpt-4o-mini) serves as generator, judge and consolidator. The judge could be biased.
- Baselines run with default settings.
- LongMemEval compares only against Full-context and Nemori.
- No variance, seeds or significance tests are reported.
- Multi-hop and F1/BLEU results are mixed.
- The causal threshold δ and the intent classifier's accuracy are not reported.

- **Eq. 3:** the event-node tuple.
- **Eq. 4:** RRF anchor fusion.
- **Eq. 5–6:** the transition score, which combines structural alignment (intent-weighted edge type) with semantic affinity. This is the technical core.

  - An intent class T_q ∈ {WHY, WHEN, ENTITY}, from a "lightweight classifier". It acts as the "steering wheel".
  - A temporal parse [τ_s, τ_e], where a temporal tagger resolves relative expressions ("last Friday") into absolute time windows.
  - A dense query embedding q⃗ and sparse keywords q_key.
- **Stage 2 — anchor identification.** Dense, lexical and temporal signals are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al. 2009). Eq. 4: S_anchor = TopK Σ_{m∈{vec,key,time}} 1/(k + r_m(n)).
- **Stage 3 — Adaptive Traversal Policy.** This is a heuristic beam search from the anchors.
  - Transition score (Eq. 5): S(n_j|n_i,q) = exp(λ1·φ(type(e_ij),T_q) + λ2·sim(n⃗_j,q⃗)).
  - Structural alignment (Eq. 6): φ(r,T_q) = w_{T_q}ᵀ·1_r. Here w_{T_q} is an intent-specific weight vector and 1_r is the one-hot edge type.
  - Example: CAUSAL edges get high weight for WHY queries.
  - Algorithm 1: frontier expansion up to MaxDepth. The cumulative score is score_v = score_u·γ + s_uv, with decay γ. The beam keeps the top-k per step. Traversal stops when a visited-node budget is reached.
- **Stage 4 — narrative synthesis via graph linearization:**
  1. *Topological ordering.* WHEN queries are sorted by timestamp. WHY queries are topologically sorted on causal edges, so causes precede effects.
  2. *Context scaffolding with provenance (Eq. 7).* Each node becomes `<t:τ_i> content <ref:id>`, and these are concatenated. This is meant to reduce hallucination and make the LLM "an interpreter of evidence rather than a creative writer".
  3. *Salience-based token budgeting.* Scores from Eq. 5 set a dynamic budget. Low-salience nodes are collapsed into "brevity codes" (e.g., "...3 intermediate events...").

### 3.4 Memory evolution: dual stream (pp. 6–7; Algorithms 2–3 on p. 6)
- **Rationale:** it is motivated by Complementary Learning Systems theory (Kumaran et al. 2016).
- **Fast path, "synaptic ingestion" (Alg. 2):**
  - Segment the event.
  - Add a temporal edge from the previous node.
  - Compute the embedding and add it to the vector DB.
  - Enqueue the node ID.
  - No blocking LLM reasoning happens here.
- **Slow path, "structural consolidation" (Alg. 3, Eq. 8):**
  - A background worker dequeues node IDs.
  - It takes the 2-hop neighborhood.
  - It prompts an LLM Φ to infer E_new = Φ_reason(N(n_t), H_history).
  - It adds the resulting Causal and Entity edges. The paper describes this as trading compute time for relational depth.

### 3.5 Implementation (p. 6)
- Three layers: storage, retrieval and application.
- The storage layer abstracts typed graph, dense-vector and sparse-keyword backends. Backends are swappable, e.g. in-memory versus production graph/vector DBs.
- Utility modules handle episodic segmentation and temporal normalization.

### Hyperparameters (Table 6, p. 13)
These were "empirically optimized on the LoCoMo benchmark".

| Group | Setting |
|---|---|
| Embedding | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d, default); text-embedding-3-small (1536-d, optional) |
| LLM | gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.0 |
| Retrieval | RRF k = 60; vector top-K = 20; keyword fusion weight 2.0–5.0; similarity threshold 0.10–0.30 |
| Traversal | max depth 5 hops; max nodes 200; drop threshold 0.15 |
| Adaptive weights | λ1 = 1.0 (base); λ2 = 0.3–0.7 |
| Intent weights | w_entity 2.5–6.0; w_temporal 0.5–4.0; w_causal 3.0–5.0; w_phrase 2.5–5.0 |

- The beam width and γ are not given in Table 6 (the extracted text shows none).
- Tuning on LoCoMo and then evaluating on it is a point a committee could press.

### Prompts (Appendix C, pp. 13–14)
- **Event extraction:** a strict-JSON prompt that returns entities, topic, relationships, semantic_facts, dates_mentioned and summary.
- **Adaptive QA prompt:**
  - It answers only from context. If the answer is absent it must say "Information not found". Answers are concise (1–10 words).
  - It injects a dynamic instruction chosen by the router: Multi-hop, Temporal (output dates as "D Month YYYY"), Open-domain/inference, or Single-hop.
  - The authors state this uses no oracle labels.
- **LLM-judge prompt:**
  - It scores 0.0–1.0 on the scale 1.0 / 0.8 / 0.6 / 0.4 / 0.2 / 0.0.
  - It accepts relative times that resolve to the same period.
  - For adversarial "Unanswerable" gold answers, any hallucinated fact scores 0.

### Alternatives mentioned
- Optional OpenAI embeddings.
- Swappable storage backends.
- The graph-schema flexibility discussed in the case study (p. 15).
- No explicit design-alternative comparisons (e.g., a different traversal algorithm) are reported beyond the ablations.

## (5) Datasets (pp. 6–7, 15)
- **LoCoMo** (Maharana et al. 2024): ultra-long multi-session conversations, "average length of 9K tokens". It targets long-range temporal and causal retrieval.
  - The full benchmark was used, with five categories (Table 7, p. 15): Single-Hop 841, Adversarial 446, Temporal 321, Multi-Hop 282, Open-Domain 96. The total is 1,986 questions.
  - No train/test split is described. Nothing is trained, but hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo (p. 13).
- **LongMemEval** (Wu et al. 2024): a stress-test benchmark with average context over 100K tokens. Six question types appear in Table 2 (p. 8). The paper gives no question counts or split information.
- **Preprocessing:** event segmentation, LLM JSON extraction, and temporal normalization. For example, "yesterday" is resolved to a date at ingestion (pp. 15–16).

## (6) Metrics and baselines
- **Primary metric:** LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al. 2023). The judge is gpt-4o-mini at temperature 0, with the rubric above (pp. 7, 14, 15).
- **Secondary metrics:** token-level F1 and BLEU-1 (Papineni et al. 2002). No formulas are given (p. 7).
- **Systems metrics:** memory build time (hours), tokens per query (k), and query latency (s) (p. 8).
- **Baselines (p. 7):**
  - Full Context (the whole history in the prompt, up to gpt-4o-mini's 128k limit).
  - A-MEM (Zettelkasten-like, self-evolving).
  - Nemori ("predict-calibrate" episodic segmentation; the paper calls it graph-based).
  - MemoryOS (hierarchical storage OS).
- **Fairness protocol (p. 15):** the same gpt-4o-mini backbone for all, official default hyperparameters for baselines, and identical judge settings.
- **Metric validation (Appendix F, pp. 16–18):**
  - Table 10 gives seven hand-built cases where F1/BLEU-1 give false rewards or false penalties.
  - "compatible" vs "not compatible" gets F1 0.857. "John" vs "Sarah" gets 0.750. "14:00" vs "2 PM" gets 0.
  - The authors use this to justify the judge over lexical metrics.

## (7) Main results
**Table 1 — LoCoMo, Judge score (p. 7):**

| Method | Multi-Hop | Temporal | Open-Domain | Single-Hop | Adversarial | Overall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full Context | 0.468 | 0.562 | 0.486 | 0.630 | 0.205 | 0.481 |
| A-MEM | 0.495 | 0.474 | 0.385 | 0.653 | 0.616 | 0.580 |
| MemoryOS | 0.552 | 0.422 | 0.504 | 0.674 | 0.428 | 0.553 |
| Nemori | 0.569 | 0.649 | 0.485 | 0.764 | 0.325 | 0.590 |
| **MAGMA** | 0.528 | 0.650 | 0.517 | 0.776 | 0.742 | **0.700** |

- The authors report relative gains of 18.6% to 45.5% over the baselines (p. 7).
- They highlight the temporal result (credited to a "Temporal Inference Engine") and the adversarial result (0.742).
- They attribute the adversarial robustness to the policy avoiding "semantically similar yet structurally irrelevant distractors" (p. 7).
- **MAGMA is not best on Multi-Hop.** Nemori scores 0.569 and MemoryOS 0.552, against 0.528 for MAGMA.

**Table 2 — LongMemEval accuracy (p. 8):**

| Question type | Full-context (101K tokens) | Nemori (3.7–4.8K) | MAGMA (0.7–4.2K) |
|---|---|---|---|
| single-session-preference | 6.7% | 62.7% | 73.3% |
| single-session-assistant | 89.3% | 73.2% | 83.9% |
| temporal-reasoning | 42.1% | 43.0% | 45.1% |
| multi-session | 38.3% | 51.4% | 50.4% |
| knowledge-update | 78.2% | 52.6% | 66.7% |
| single-session-user | 78.6% | 77.7% | 72.9% |
| **Average** | 55.0% | 56.2% | **61.2%** |

- The authors claim more than 95% token reduction versus full context, with competitive accuracy (p. 7).
- Full-context is better than MAGMA on single-session-assistant, knowledge-update and single-session-user.
- Nemori is better on multi-session and single-session-user. Only Full-context and Nemori are compared here, not A-MEM or MemoryOS.
- **Check:** the simple mean of MAGMA's six rows is about 65.4, not 61.2. The reported averages are presumably weighted by question counts, but the paper does not say so. A committee member could raise this.

**Table 3 — Efficiency (p. 8):**

| Method | Build time (h) | Tokens/query (k) | Latency (s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full Context | N/A | 8.53 | 1.74 |
| A-MEM | 1.01 | 2.62 | 2.26 |
| MemoryOS | 0.91 | 4.76 | 32.68 |
| Nemori | 0.29 | 3.46 | 2.59 |
| MAGMA | 0.39 | 3.37 | **1.47** |

- MAGMA has the lowest latency, "about 40% faster than … A-MEM".
- A-MEM has the lowest token use (2.62k), but the authors say it sacrifices reasoning depth.
- Nemori builds faster (0.29 h vs 0.39 h).
- The authors credit the latency to early pruning by the traversal policy and to the dual-stream design.

**Table 4 — Ablation, leave-one-out on LoCoMo (p. 8):**

| Variant | Judge | F1 | BLEU-1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| w/o Adaptive Policy | 0.637 | 0.413 | 0.357 |
| w/o Causal Links | 0.644 | 0.439 | 0.354 |
| w/o Temporal Backbone | 0.647 | 0.438 | 0.349 |
| w/o Entity Links | 0.666 | 0.451 | 0.363 |
| Full | 0.700 | 0.467 | 0.378 |

- Removing the Adaptive Policy hurts most. Causal and Temporal matter about equally. Entity matters least.

**Table 5 — Single-graph ablation (p. 9):**

| Variant | Overall | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Causal only | 0.590 | Best single graph overall |
| Temporal only | 0.577 | Best single graph on temporal (0.620) |
| Entity only | 0.531 | Lowest overall; weak on temporal and adversarial |
| Full MAGMA | 0.700 | |

- No single graph exceeds 0.60, so the relation types are complementary (p. 9).
- The ablations only cover Causal, Temporal and Entity. The semantic graph is not ablated.

**Table 9 — F1/BLEU-1 on LoCoMo (p. 17):**

| Method | Overall F1 / BLEU-1 |
|---|---|
| Nemori | 0.502 / 0.403 |
| MAGMA | 0.467 / 0.378 |
| MemoryOS | 0.413 / 0.355 |
| Full Context | 0.140 / 0.096 |
| A-MEM | 0.116 / 0.074 |

- MAGMA is not best under lexical metrics. Nemori leads overall, and MAGMA is far behind on Multi-Hop F1 (0.264 vs 0.363–0.365).
- The authors justify the judge metric in Appendix F. Table 9 has no Adversarial column.

**Case study (Appendix E, pp. 15–16; Table 8):** three LoCoMo examples about "Melanie".
1. **Instruments (Q1).** MAGMA answers "Clarinet and Violin". It aggregated an entity-centric neighborhood. A-MEM lost the violin detail to summarization, and others found only the clarinet.
2. **Number of children (Q2).** MAGMA answers "at least three": two in a photo, plus a distinct son/brother. Baselines answered "two".
3. **Hike date (Q3).** MAGMA answers "19 October 2023". It resolved "yesterday" against the session date of 20 October. A-MEM copied the session date. MemoryOS gave "29 December 2025".

## (8) Limitations and future work (p. 9)
1. **LLM-dependent graph quality.** Consolidation relies on LLM inference, so extraction errors and hallucinations can create spurious or missing edges and propagate downstream. The authors cite structured prompts and "conservative inference thresholds" as mitigation.
2. **Complexity.** Multiple graphs and dual-stream processing add storage and engineering overhead ("a little higher"). This may limit use in resource-constrained settings.
3. **Narrow evaluation.** Only conversational and agentic benchmarks are covered. Extending to multimodal agents or heterogeneous observation streams "may require additional adaptation and calibration" (future work).

**Threats to validity the authors do not discuss** (my observations, flagged as such):
- Hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo, which is also the main test set.
- A single backbone (gpt-4o-mini) serves as generator, judge and consolidator. The judge could be biased.
- Baselines run with default settings.
- LongMemEval compares only against Full-context and Nemori.
- No variance, seeds or significance tests are reported.
- Multi-hop and F1/BLEU results are mixed.
- The causal threshold δ and the intent classifier's accuracy are not reported.

## (9) Related work (Section 2 on pp. 2–3; Appendix A on pp. 12–13)
- **Context-window extension:** Longformer (Beltagy 2020), ALiBi (Press 2021), LM2 (Kang 2025c), MemoRAG (Qian 2025). These do not address the continual, write-back nature of agent memory.
- **RAG:** Lewis et al. 2020, LongRAG, M-RAG, RAGO, Self-Correcting RAG, HippoRAG-style "From RAG to Memory" (Gutiérrez 2025). RAG typically assumes a static corpus.
- **MAG / agent memory systems:**
  - MemoryBank, Generative Agents (Park 2023), MemGPT (Packer 2023), MemoryOS (Kang 2025), MemOS (Li 2025), Hippocampus (Li 2026), Mem0 (Chhikara 2025), MIRIX, Nemori, Zep.
  - Zep is a temporal knowledge-graph engine ("Graphiti").
- **Structured memory:**
  - Think-in-Memory (TiM) stores chains of thought.
  - A-MEM uses Zettelkasten-style linking.
  - GraphRAG (Edge 2024) uses entity graphs with community summaries.
- **Causal reasoning and evaluation:** Kiciman et al. 2023, Jin et al. 2023 (CLadder), LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng 2023).
- **Other key citations:** Cormack 2009 (RRF), Johnson 2019 (FAISS), Kumaran 2016 (CLS theory), Liu 2024 (Lost in the Middle).
- **Gap claimed:** no prior system disentangles semantic, temporal, causal and entity relations with intent-aware traversal.

## (10) Central equations, figures and diagrams
- **Eq. 1–2:** the MAG feedback loop.
- **Eq. 3:** the event-node tuple.
- **Eq. 4:** RRF anchor fusion.
- **Eq. 5–6:** the transition score, which combines structural alignment (intent-weighted edge type) with semantic affinity. This is the technical core.
- **Eq. 7:** linearized context with timestamps and provenance.
- **Eq. 8:** LLM-based consolidation.
- **Fig. 1 (p. 2):** the MAG loop.
- **Fig. 2 (p. 3):** the three-layer architecture. The query path runs Intent-Aware Router → Anchor Identification with RRF → Adaptive Traversal Policy → Context Synthesizer → LLM response. The write path runs event segmentation → dense/sparse embedding → semantic, temporal and entity linking, with an async queue feeding LLM causal inference.
- **Fig. 3 (p. 5):** the query pipeline. Semantic, lexical and temporal signals feed RRF to anchors, and policy weights then guide traversal over the semantic, temporal, causal and entity views.
- **Algorithms 1–3:** beam-search retrieval, fast-path ingestion, and slow-path consolidation.
- **Inconsistencies a student should know:**
  - The text lists T_q ∈ {WHY, WHEN, ENTITY}, but the QA prompt uses categories such as Multi-hop, Temporal and Open-domain.
  - Table 6 lists a "w_phrase" weight that is not defined in the main text.
  - Algorithm 1 as printed shows the Phase 1 anchor step using only vector and keyword search.

## Jargon to know
- Memory-Augmented Generation (MAG) vs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
- Agentic memory
- Long-horizon reasoning
- Lost-in-the-middle; context decay; attention dilution
- Context window; token budget

arguments.question:
Um sistema RAG simples guarda cada mensagem de uma conversa longa como um embedding (por exemplo, `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`). Na hora da pergunta, ele recupera as top-$K$ mensagens por similaridade de cosseno com a pergunta.

Pergunta do usuário: *"O que a Melanie fez no dia seguinte à festa?"*

Qual é o resultado mais provável?

options.label: Traz mensagens sobre festas e sobre a Melanie, não necessariamente o evento seguinte à festa
Não traz nada, pois só recupera mensagens que contêm as mesmas palavras da pergunta
Traz o evento certo, mas só como vetor, sem o texto para o LLM ler
Traz o evento certo, pois o embedding registra a ordem das mensagens na conversa

arguments.explanation:
O embedding de uma mensagem codifica o **significado do texto dela**, e mais nada. Ele não registra quando a mensagem aconteceu nem o que veio antes ou depois. A similaridade de cosseno com a pergunta favorece mensagens que *falam sobre* festas e sobre a Melanie. O evento do dia seguinte pode não ter nada a ver com festa (por exemplo, "fui fazer uma trilha") e por isso fica com similaridade baixa.

As outras opções erram assim:
- **(b)** descreve busca esparsa por palavra-chave (tipo BM25). A busca densa com embeddings justamente pega sinônimos e paráfrases.
- **(c)** O vetor serve só de índice. O banco devolve o texto original associado a ele.
- **(d)** Cada mensagem é codificada de forma independente, sem posição na conversa.

Essa é a motivação central do MAGMA: a similaridade semântica não captura relações **temporais** nem **causais**. Daí as arestas temporais explícitas e o *temporal parse* no roteador (pp. 1–4).
